title: The Art of Career Management
author: Ian Hallett
summary: Ian Hallett synthesizes research on executive career trajectories to argue that steady excellence in one's current role is a weak predictor of promotion readiness and can even be actively counterproductive, citing a Quarterly Journal of Economics study of 131 companies finding that the strongest pre-promotion sales performers became the worst-performing managers afterward. Against this, he draws on the ten-year CEO Genome Project's finding that 97% of executives who reached the top job fastest had made at least one 'career catapult': a sideways or downward move, an underqualified stretch role, or taking on a failing business, each of which builds a specific capability (deciding under incomplete information, running a full P&L, delegating to people who know more than you) years before the next level demands it. Mary Barra's real path to GM's chief executive seat, via a 2009 sideways move into HR during the company's bankruptcy, is offered as a concrete illustration that these moves rarely look like a deliberate plan at the time. Hallett pairs capability with sponsorship, citing a Harvard Business Review study on the Catalyst survey showing mentorship (cheap, common advice) is frequently mistaken for sponsorship (costly, career-making advocacy at the moment a role is decided), and closes with two scripted conversations readers can use to test whether they have a sponsor and to actively request a stretch assignment, alongside an explicit warning that bold moves have an unmeasured failure rate and can backfire badly if taken on without real authority or budget.
points: Central finding, from a Quarterly Journal of Economics study of 131 companies: strong current-role performance is a weak or even negative predictor of promotion success — doubling pre-promotion sales corresponded to a 7.5% fall in the resulting manager's team performance.

The CEO Genome Project (17,000+ executive assessments) found 97% of the fastest-promoted executives ('sprinters') had made at least one 'career catapult' — a sideways/downward move, an underqualified stretch role, or taking on a failing business — with pedigree (elite MBAs) explaining little of the difference.

Mary Barra's 2009 sideways move into GM's HR role during the company's bankruptcy is used as a real-world case showing catapult moves rarely look like a deliberate career plan at the time but build exactly the experience the next level requires.

Citing a Harvard Business Review study on a Catalyst survey of 4,000+ high potentials, Hallett distinguishes mentorship (cheap, common advice) from sponsorship (costly advocacy that puts someone's standing behind you at the moment a role is appointed) as the less-discussed second half of career advancement.

He supplies two direct, scripted conversations — one asking a manager for a struggling assignment, one asking a senior backer to sponsor a P&L role — plus an explicit caution that bold moves have an unmeasured failure rate and can be damaging if taken on without real authority or budget.
quotes: Among the executives who reached the chief executive's job fastest, 97% had made at least one bold career move: a step sideways or down, a move into a job they were not quite ready for, or taking on a failing business.
The stronger a manager's own sales had been beforehand, the worse their team performed under them. A doubling of pre-promotion sales corresponded to a 7.5% fall in that manager's value added.
So a career built on outperforming everyone at your own level earns you a promotion into a job you cannot yet do.

In 2009 none of that looked like a plan. What the HR job gave her was the labour relations, the talent pipeline, and the internal politics of a company in distress, which was exactly the experience a chief executive of GM would later need.
Advice is cheap to give and pleasant to receive, which is why there is so much of it. Advocacy costs the giver something, which is why you have to ask for it directly.
The final sentence gives the other person permission to decline, and their answer tells you within a minute whether you have a sponsor.
Take on a mess without the authority or the budget to fix it, and you will be accountable for an outcome you have no way to change.
